title: Where do IP addresses come from?
summary: Watch a PC get its IP address with DHCP, inspect every message, then fix a network where it's gone wrong.
simplification: Simplified simulation: real DHCP messages carry more fields, and clients differ in small details (for example, some ask the server to reply directly instead of by broadcast). The four-step exchange, ports, addresses and options shown here are accurate.

discover.name: DHCP Discover
discover.say: Is there a DHCP server out there? I need an IP address!
discover.explain: The PC has no address and doesn't know where the DHCP server is, so it shouts to everyone on the local network. The switch copies broadcasts out of every port.

reactions.server: A Discover! I'll offer an address.
reactions.router: A broadcast. Routers don't pass these on to other networks, so I ignore it.

fields.name: Message type
fields.explain: Which of the four DHCP steps this is.

fields.name: Source IP
fields.explain: The PC has no address yet, so it uses 'nobody'.

fields.name: Destination IP
fields.explain: Broadcast: delivered to every device on this local network.

fields.name: Source MAC
fields.explain: The PC's network card's hardware address. This is how the server will recognise it.

fields.name: Destination MAC
fields.explain: The broadcast MAC address. Every device's network card accepts it.

fields.name: UDP ports
fields.explain: DHCP clients send from port 68 to servers on port 67.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.explain: A random number. Replies carry the same ID so the PC can match them to its request.

offer.name: DHCP Offer
offer.say: You can have 192.168.1.50 for 24 hours. Here are the settings you'll need.
offer.explain: The server picks a free address from its pool and offers it, together with the subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server the PC needs.

reactions.pc: An offer! Let me take a look.

fields.name: Message type
fields.explain: Step 2: an offer.

fields.name: Offered address
fields.explain: The 'your IP address' (yiaddr) field: the address being offered.

fields.name: Lease time
fields.explain: Option 51. How long the PC may use the address before renewing.

fields.name: Subnet mask
fields.explain: Option 1. Which addresses count as 'local' (192.168.1.x).

fields.name: Router (gateway)
fields.explain: Option 3. Where to send traffic for other networks, like the internet.

fields.name: DNS server
fields.explain: Option 6. Who to ask to turn names into IP addresses.

fields.name: Server identifier
fields.explain: Option 54. Which server made this offer.

fields.name: Destination IP
fields.explain: Broadcast here. Some clients ask for a direct (unicast) reply instead; either way it's aimed at the PC's MAC address.

fields.name: UDP ports
fields.explain: Server port 67 back to client port 68.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.explain: Same as the Discover, so the PC knows this answers its question.

request.name: DHCP Request
request.say: Yes please! I'll take 192.168.1.50 from server 192.168.1.2.
request.explain: The PC accepts the offer. It still broadcasts, so that if several servers made offers, they all learn which one was chosen and the others can release their addresses.

reactions.server: It accepted my offer. Let me confirm it.

fields.name: Message type
fields.explain: Step 3: accepting an offer.

fields.name: Requested address
fields.explain: Option 50. The address the PC wants.

fields.name: Server identifier
fields.explain: Option 54. Which server's offer was accepted. Any other server that made an offer now knows to release it.

fields.name: Source IP
fields.explain: Still no address: it isn't the PC's until the server confirms.

fields.name: Destination IP
fields.explain: Broadcast, so every DHCP server hears the decision.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.explain: Same conversation, same ID.

ack.name: DHCP Acknowledge
ack.explain: The server records the lease and confirms it. The PC configures its network card and can now talk to the gateway and beyond.

reactions.pc: I have an address! Setting up 192.168.1.50 now.
reactions.router: Ignoring the broadcast, but I'll see this PC's traffic soon.

fields.name: Message type
fields.explain: Step 4: the lease is confirmed.

fields.name: Your address
fields.explain: Now officially the PC's for the lease time.

fields.name: Lease time
fields.explain: The PC will try to renew it after about half the lease time.

fields.name: Subnet mask / gateway / DNS
fields.explain: The settings the PC now applies.

fields.name: Next step (not shown)
fields.explain: Many clients then quickly check that no other device is already using the address before they start using it.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.explain: Matches the whole conversation.

guided.label: Guided
guided.intro: Press Play (or Step) and watch the PC get an address. Click any message to inspect it. Turn on protocol details for the technical fields.
guided.debrief: That's the whole of DHCP: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (often remembered as DORA). The PC started with no address, found a server by broadcasting, and left with an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server: everything it needs to use the network. Next, try Practice mode and predict each step before it happens.

practice.label: Practice
practice.intro: Same network, but now you predict what happens before each message is sent. Get it right to continue.

discover.q: The PC has no IP address yet. Who does it send its first DHCP message to?
options: Everyone on the local network (a broadcast)
The router, which forwards it to the internet
discover.why: It doesn't know where any server is yet, so it broadcasts to 255.255.255.255 and the switch floods it out of every port.

offer.q: What will the server's Offer contain?
options: A password to join the network
A proposed IP address plus settings like the subnet mask, gateway and DNS server
A list of websites the PC is allowed to visit
offer.why: The offer is a complete network configuration: address, mask, gateway, DNS and how long the lease lasts.

request.q: The PC has an offer from 192.168.1.2. Why does it broadcast its Request instead of sending it only to that server?
options: So every DHCP server learns which offer was accepted and others can release theirs
Because broadcasts are faster than direct messages
It doesn't: the Request goes only to the router
request.why: Networks can have more than one DHCP server. Broadcasting the decision (with the chosen server's identifier) lets the others release the addresses they offered.

ack.q: What happens after the server sends its Acknowledge?
options: The PC must restart to use the address
The PC starts using the address for the length of the lease
The server waits for another Discover before confirming
ack.why: The ACK confirms the lease. The PC applies the address and settings, and later renews the lease before it expires.

practice.debrief: You predicted every step of DORA. The key ideas: the PC broadcasts because it has no address and doesn't know where the server is; the offer is a full configuration; the Request is broadcast so every server hears the decision; the ACK makes it official. Ready for Challenge mode?

challenge.label: Challenge
challenge.intro: Monday, 9am. A user says their PC 'has no internet'. Other people are starting to complain too. Use the tools to find out why, fix it properly, then explain the root cause.
hints: Start with the PC itself: what IP address does it have?
An address starting 169.254 means the PC asked DHCP for an address and nobody answered. Who should have answered?
Check the DHCP server, fix what you find, then make the PC ask again.

outcomes.finding: The PC has a 169.254.x.x address. That's a self-assigned (APIPA) address: Windows and macOS pick one when they ask DHCP for an address and get no reply.
The PC has a proper 192.168.1.x address with a gateway and DNS server.

tools.label: Check the cable and network link

outcomes.output:
Link status: Connected (1 Gbps)
Switch port 3: up
outcomes.finding: The physical connection is fine, so the problem is higher up than cables.

outcomes.output:
Pinging 192.168.1.1 with 32 bytes of data:
Request timed out.
Request timed out.
Request timed out.
Request timed out.
outcomes.finding: No reply. With a 169.254 address the PC isn't part of the 192.168.1.x network at all, so it can't reach the gateway.

outcomes.output:
Pinging 192.168.1.1 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64
Reply from 192.168.1.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64
outcomes.finding: The gateway replies, so the PC is on the network.

outcomes.output: The operation failed: DHCP is not enabled on this adapter (it has a manually set address).
outcomes.finding: Renewing does nothing while the address is set by hand.

outcomes.output:
Sending DHCP Discover…
No DHCP server responded. Keeping address {pc.ip}.
outcomes.finding: The Discover goes out, but nothing answers it. The PC is asking correctly; the problem is on the server side.
The full DORA exchange worked and the PC got a proper address.

tools.label: Check the DHCP service on the server

outcomes.finding: The DHCP service is stopped, so nobody is answering Discover messages. That explains why every PC is getting 169.254 addresses.

outcomes.output:
Starting DHCP Server service… done.
Status: Running
outcomes.finding: The service is running again, but the PC won't notice until it asks for an address again.

tools.label: Type in a fixed IP address on the PC

outcomes.finding: This PC can reach the network now, but this is a workaround, not a fix. Everyone else still gets 169.254 addresses, and hand-picked addresses can clash with ones DHCP hands out later.

tools.label: Set the PC back to automatic (DHCP)

outcomes.output: Adapter set to obtain an address automatically.
outcomes.finding: Back on DHCP. Ask for a new address to get one.

outcomes.output: The adapter is already set to obtain an address automatically.

options: The PC's network cable was unplugged
The DHCP service on the server had stopped
The PC's firewall was blocking the internet
rootCause.why: The link was up, the PC was sending Discovers, and nothing answered because the DHCP service was stopped. DNS and firewalls can't explain a 169.254 address.

challenge.debrief: Root cause: the DHCP service had stopped, so every PC that asked for an address got silence and fell back to a 169.254 self-assigned address. The evidence chain was: a 169.254 address (no DHCP answer), a working link (not a cable problem), a Discover that went out with no reply (the server side), and finally a stopped service. Restarting it fixed every PC at once. Typing in a fixed address would have fixed just one PC and hidden the real problem. In a real job you'd also ask why the service stopped and set up monitoring so you hear about it before users do.
